samples.summary: On a non-HTTPS deployment the `wafflebase_cli_confirm` cookie loses its `__Host-` prefix, so anyone who can plant a cookie on the origin can forge the human confirmation the new headers exist to protect
samples.evidence: `issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE)` names the cookie via `loginCookieName` (github-auth.guard.ts:92-97), which only adds `__Host-` when `secureCookies()` is true (line 71-75: NODE_ENV=production or an https `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`). On any plain-http deployment the wire name is the bare `wafflebase_cli_confirm`, an ordinary host cookie. An attacker who can write the victim's cookie jar for that origin (sibling subdomain, or a network position on cleartext http) sets `wafflebase_cli_confirm=X` and then sends the victim a single link `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker listener>&nonce=…&code_challenge=…&cli_confirm=X`. `hasConfirmation` (line 313-325) compares the query half against the cookie half and both are the attacker's, so the guard skips the interstitial entirely, mints the state and redirects straight to GitHub — the consent page the victim never sees, and the code is delivered to the attacker's loopback port. The delta hardens that page against click theft while the click itself remains skippable on these deployments. Note the same `__Host-` caveat is documented for the *state* cookie (loginCookieName's comment) but not for the confirm cookie, whose whole value is being unforgeable from a link.

samples.summary: No `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` anywhere in the backend, including the unauthenticated `/images/:id` route that echoes user-uploaded bytes from the same origin as the consent page and the session cookie
samples.evidence: The delta's own rationale states there is no helmet or global header layer in this app, and adds headers to exactly one response. Grepping the backend for `nosniff` / `X-Content-Type-Options` returns nothing: `image.controller.ts:71-76` sets only `Content-Type` (from the id extension) and a one-year public cache, and `file-response.util.ts:18-48` returns only `contentType`/`disposition`. Both serve bytes an authenticated user uploaded, on the backend origin — the same origin that serves the CLI consent page and the `wafflebase_session` cookie. A stored `text/html` rendered on that origin would read the consent page's confirm token straight out of the DOM and defeat the entire click gate, so the origin's sniffing posture is load-bearing for the control this delta hardens. The MIME is forced from server-held state in both places, so this is defence-in-depth for sniffing browsers rather than a live vector — hence minor.
searchedFor: grep for text/html and <!DOCTYPE across packages

samples.summary: The consent page's CSP carries only `frame-ancestors`; `default-src`/`script-src`/`base-uri`/`form-action` are unset, so the page has no second line of defence if its markup ever gains a dynamic value
samples.evidence: `'Content-Security-Policy': "frame-ancestors 'none'"` (auth.controller.ts:139) restricts embedding only. The page today is safe because every interpolated value (`href`, `port`) goes through `escapeHtml` (line 39-46) and `URLSearchParams`, but this is the one HTML response the backend serves and it embeds a single-use confirm token; `default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'` would cost nothing here (no scripts, no forms, one inline <style>) and would keep an injected `<script>` or a rewritten `<base>` from exfiltrating that token. Preference-level hardening, not a live vector.

verdict.reason: Every claimed element checks out in the repository. CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE is issued through issueLoginCookie -> loginCookieName (github-auth.guard.ts:284, 344, 92-97), which applies __Host- only when secureCookies() is true (lines 71-75: NODE_ENV=production or an https GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL). On a plain-http origin the wire name is the bare wafflebase_cli_confirm, and the guard's own comment (lines 86-90) admits there is then "no defence against an attacker who can plant cookies on that origin". hasConfirmation (lines 313-325) is a bare double-submit with no secondary binding: it compares only query cli_confirm to that cookie, with nothing tying either half to the port, nonce, or challenge (contrast the browser state, which at least gets stateSignature at line 149). An attacker who can write the victim's cookie jar for the origin (sibling subdomain, or cleartext-http position) sets both halves, so hasConfirmation returns true, line 290-298 clears the confirm cookie, mints the CLI state with the attacker's port, and super.canActivate redirects to GitHub — the interstitial (auth.controller.ts:119-146) never renders. The callback does not recover the gate: verifyCallbackState (auth.controller.ts:311-321) only checks the CLI_STATE_COOKIE binding that this same guarded start just minted in the victim's browser, then redirects the code to http://127.0.0.1:<attacker port> (auth.controller.ts:259-261). The plain-http configuration is documented and supported, not hypothetical (packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:42 and packages/backend/README.md:31 both ship http:// callback URLs). No refutation ground applies: the code is present as described, no guard elsewhere makes it unreachable, and a forgeable human-consent gate yielding an authorization code for the victim's account is core auth/CSRF territory for this lens.

finding.summary: CLI consent interstitial is framable — no X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors anywhere in the backend, so the new "human confirmation" binding is clickjackable from any same-site page
finding.evidence: `githubAuth` renders the new consent page with `res.type('html').send(...)` (auth.controller.ts:122-127) and no framing headers. I grepped the whole `packages/` tree for `helmet|X-Frame-Options|frame-ancestors|Content-Security-Policy|frameguard` and the only hit is a spell dictionary — the app sets none globally either (packages/backend/src/main.ts has no helmet). This page is documented as the *last* line of defence for the CLI flow: the guard's own comment (github-auth.guard.ts:217-224) says the nonce, the PKCE challenge and the browser-binding cookie are all held by whoever *wrote* the start URL, so only the deliberate click on this page stops `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker's listener>&nonce=…&code_challenge=…`. Attack: attacker frames `https://api.example.com/auth/github?mode=cli&port=…` and UI-redresses the `<a class="continue">` link so the victim clicks it; the login proceeds to GitHub and the victim's code is delivered to the attacker's loopback listener. Mitigation that partially holds: `wafflebase_cli_confirm` is `SameSite=Lax`, so in a *cross-site* iframe it is not sent on the framed click and the gate re-renders. But `SameSite` is eTLD+1-based, and this deployment explicitly assumes frontend and backend share eTLD+1 (auth.controller.ts:468 comment), so any same-site page — the frontend itself, a sibling subdomain, an HTML injection on either — is same-site, the Lax cookie *is* sent, and the clickjack succeeds. `__Host-` does not prevent framing. Fix: send `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`) on this response, and preferably require a POST for the continue action.

verdict.reason: The finding claims the CLI consent interstitial is served with no anti-framing headers and that no X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors exists anywhere in the backend. Both premises are false. packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:137-141 sets exactly the requested mitigation on this very response — `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`, plus `Cache-Control: no-store` — chained on `res` between `.type('html')` (line 124) and `.send(this.renderCliConsent(...))` (line 144). The reviewer's quoted evidence ("res.type('html').send(...)" at 122-127 with no headers) misreads a single chained expression, and the claimed repo-wide grep result ("only hit is a spell dictionary") is contradicted by hits in auth.controller.ts:138-139 and auth.controller.spec.ts:614-615. Coverage is complete rather than incidental: renderCliConsent has exactly one call site (auth.controller.ts:144), reachable only when the guard sets req.__cliConsent (github-auth.guard.ts:286), so there is no alternate unheadered render path. The behaviour is pinned by a regression test at auth.controller.spec.ts:609-619, whose comment (603-608) anticipates the reviewer's exact threat model (same-site framing under shared eTLD+1, SameSite=Lax covering only cross-site framers, no helmet in this app). The lack of a global helmet layer is real but immaterial because the route carries the refusal itself. The secondary "preferably require a POST" suggestion is hardening beyond the stated blocking claim and does not stand alone once the anti-framing defence is present and tested.
